nodes.title: Part 1: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 1. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A newly-appointed cloud auditor is asked to explain the primary purpose of the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM). Which description is MOST accurate?
flashcards.back: The Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) is a cybersecurity control framework maintained by the Cloud Security Alliance. It organises controls into domains (17 in v4) and cross-maps them to widely-used standards such as ISO/IEC 27001/27002, NIST SP 800-53, PCI DSS, HIPAA and COBIT so cloud providers and customers can evaluate cloud security against familiar baselines. It is not a legal contract, a commercial ranking, or an automated remediation tool.

flashcards.front: During due diligence, a customer asks a cloud service provider (CSP) to disclose how it implements each control in the CCM. Which artefact is specifically designed for that purpose?
flashcards.back: The CAIQ (Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire) is a set of yes/no questions aligned to the CCM domains that a CSP completes to describe how each control is implemented. It is the primary self-disclosure vehicle used for STAR Level 1 self-assessment. An SLA covers performance commitments; SOC 1 addresses financial-reporting controls; the SIG Lite is a broader third-party risk questionnaire not scoped to the CCM.

flashcards.front: The CSA STAR Registry offers three levels of assurance. Which statement correctly describes STAR Level 2?
flashcards.back: STAR has three tiers of assurance. Level 1 is a public self-assessment based on the CAIQ. Level 2 is a third-party audit resulting in either STAR Certification (based on ISO/IEC 27001 plus the CCM) or STAR Attestation (based on SOC 2 plus the CCM). Level 3 (STAR Continuous) provides ongoing assurance through automated control monitoring. There is no peer-voting tier.

flashcards.front: In an IaaS deployment, who is responsible for securing the physical hardware, the host operating system and the virtualisation layer?
flashcards.back: In the shared responsibility model for IaaS, the CSP is responsible for security 'of' the cloud — the data centre, hardware, host OS and virtualisation layer. The customer is responsible for security 'in' the cloud — the guest OS, applications, data, identity and network configuration. The SLA describes uptime and support commitments, not who owns each control; certification bodies audit the CSP but do not operate any control.

questions.q: A newly-appointed cloud auditor is asked to explain the primary purpose of the CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM). Which description is MOST accurate?
choices: A cybersecurity control framework organised into domains and mapped to industry standards, tailored to cloud computing
A contract template that cloud providers must sign before offering services to enterprise customers
A benchmarking tool that ranks cloud providers by their annual revenue and customer count
A code library that automatically remediates misconfigurations in public-cloud environments
questions.explanation: The Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) is a cybersecurity control framework maintained by the Cloud Security Alliance. It organises controls into domains (17 in v4) and cross-maps them to widely-used standards such as ISO/IEC 27001/27002, NIST SP 800-53, PCI DSS, HIPAA and COBIT so cloud providers and customers can evaluate cloud security against familiar baselines. It is not a legal contract, a commercial ranking, or an automated remediation tool.

questions.q: During due diligence, a customer asks a cloud service provider (CSP) to disclose how it implements each control in the CCM. Which artefact is specifically designed for that purpose?
choices: The service-level agreement (SLA)
The provider's SOC 1 Type 1 report
The CSA Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ)
The SIG (Standardised Information Gathering) Lite questionnaire from Shared Assessments
questions.explanation: The CAIQ (Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire) is a set of yes/no questions aligned to the CCM domains that a CSP completes to describe how each control is implemented. It is the primary self-disclosure vehicle used for STAR Level 1 self-assessment. An SLA covers performance commitments; SOC 1 addresses financial-reporting controls; the SIG Lite is a broader third-party risk questionnaire not scoped to the CCM.

questions.q: The CSA STAR Registry offers three levels of assurance. Which statement correctly describes STAR Level 2?
choices: A CSP self-assessment based on a completed CAIQ, published for public review
An independent third-party assessment resulting in STAR Certification (against ISO/IEC 27001) or STAR Attestation (based on SOC 2)
A community peer review in which other CSPs vote on a provider's security posture
A continuous-audit programme that streams control evidence from the CSP to the registry in real time
questions.explanation: STAR has three tiers of assurance. Level 1 is a public self-assessment based on the CAIQ. Level 2 is a third-party audit resulting in either STAR Certification (based on ISO/IEC 27001 plus the CCM) or STAR Attestation (based on SOC 2 plus the CCM). Level 3 (STAR Continuous) provides ongoing assurance through automated control monitoring. There is no peer-voting tier.

questions.q: In an IaaS deployment, who is responsible for securing the physical hardware, the host operating system and the virtualisation layer?
choices: The cloud customer, because they select the underlying instance types
Whichever party the SLA identifies as the operator of record for the region
The certification body that issues the CSP's STAR Attestation
The cloud service provider, because those layers are managed 'below the line' in the shared responsibility model
questions.explanation: In the shared responsibility model for IaaS, the CSP is responsible for security 'of' the cloud — the data centre, hardware, host OS and virtualisation layer. The customer is responsible for security 'in' the cloud — the guest OS, applications, data, identity and network configuration. The SLA describes uptime and support commitments, not who owns each control; certification bodies audit the CSP but do not operate any control.

nodes.title: Part 2: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 2. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A cloud auditor is reviewing a CSP's SOC 2 Type 2 report as part of an engagement. Which of the following BEST describes the scope of a SOC 2 Type 2 report?
flashcards.back: SOC 2 Type 1 assesses the suitability of the design of controls at a single point in time. SOC 2 Type 2 assesses both design AND operating effectiveness across a period (typically 6–12 months), so it provides higher assurance that controls actually work in practice. SOC 1 (not SOC 2) addresses controls relevant to financial reporting; and SOC 2 covers the five Trust Services Criteria, not physical security in isolation.

flashcards.front: Which ISO/IEC standard extends 27002 with cloud-specific information-security controls for both cloud providers and cloud customers?
flashcards.back: ISO/IEC 27017 is the code of practice that supplements ISO/IEC 27002 with information-security controls specifically for cloud services, with guidance for both cloud service providers and cloud service customers. ISO/IEC 27001 defines the ISMS management-system requirements; ISO/IEC 27018 focuses on protection of personally identifiable information (PII) in public-cloud environments; ISO/IEC 22301 is the business-continuity management standard.

flashcards.front: The CSA Cloud Data Lifecycle defines six sequential phases. Which set correctly lists them in order?
flashcards.back: The CSA cloud data lifecycle used in the CCAK body of knowledge is Create → Store → Use → Share → Archive → Destroy. Different controls (encryption, DLP, access review, retention, key destruction) apply at different phases, and auditors evaluate them phase by phase. The other sequences are ETL, generic data-management or ITIL-style lifecycles, not the CSA model.

flashcards.front: A cloud auditor identifies multi-tenancy as a top audit risk at a public CSP. Which follow-up test BEST addresses the risk?
flashcards.back: Multi-tenancy means many customers share the same underlying infrastructure, so the auditor must verify tenant-isolation controls — hypervisor segregation, storage encryption per tenant, virtual-network segmentation and identity boundaries — through configuration inspection and reliance on independent attestations such as SOC 2 or STAR. Accessing another tenant's data would itself violate isolation, sustainability reports are unrelated, and public CSPs do not expose rack-level placement to customers.

questions.q: A cloud auditor is reviewing a CSP's SOC 2 Type 2 report as part of an engagement. Which of the following BEST describes the scope of a SOC 2 Type 2 report?
choices: The design AND operating effectiveness of the CSP's controls over a defined period, typically 6 to 12 months
The design of the CSP's controls at a specific point in time only
The accuracy of the CSP's published financial statements over the previous fiscal year
The physical security of the CSP's data-centre facilities only
questions.explanation: SOC 2 Type 1 assesses the suitability of the design of controls at a single point in time. SOC 2 Type 2 assesses both design AND operating effectiveness across a period (typically 6–12 months), so it provides higher assurance that controls actually work in practice. SOC 1 (not SOC 2) addresses controls relevant to financial reporting; and SOC 2 covers the five Trust Services Criteria, not physical security in isolation.

questions.q: Which ISO/IEC standard extends 27002 with cloud-specific information-security controls for both cloud providers and cloud customers?
choices: ISO/IEC 27001
ISO/IEC 27018
ISO/IEC 22301
ISO/IEC 27017
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27017 is the code of practice that supplements ISO/IEC 27002 with information-security controls specifically for cloud services, with guidance for both cloud service providers and cloud service customers. ISO/IEC 27001 defines the ISMS management-system requirements; ISO/IEC 27018 focuses on protection of personally identifiable information (PII) in public-cloud environments; ISO/IEC 22301 is the business-continuity management standard.

questions.q: The CSA Cloud Data Lifecycle defines six sequential phases. Which set correctly lists them in order?
choices: Create → Store → Use → Share → Archive → Destroy
Ingest → Transform → Store → Analyse → Report → Purge
Collect → Classify → Encrypt → Move → Retain → Delete
Plan → Build → Deploy → Operate → Monitor → Retire
questions.explanation: The CSA cloud data lifecycle used in the CCAK body of knowledge is Create → Store → Use → Share → Archive → Destroy. Different controls (encryption, DLP, access review, retention, key destruction) apply at different phases, and auditors evaluate them phase by phase. The other sequences are ETL, generic data-management or ITIL-style lifecycles, not the CSA model.

questions.q: A cloud auditor identifies multi-tenancy as a top audit risk at a public CSP. Which follow-up test BEST addresses the risk?
choices: Verify that the CSP publishes an annual sustainability report
Evaluate the design and operating effectiveness of tenant-isolation controls (compute, storage, network and identity segregation) via inspection of configurations and third-party attestations
Ask the CSP to grant read-only access to another tenant's production data for a 30-minute walk-through
Confirm that the CSP allows the customer to select the exact physical rack their workloads run on
questions.explanation: Multi-tenancy means many customers share the same underlying infrastructure, so the auditor must verify tenant-isolation controls — hypervisor segregation, storage encryption per tenant, virtual-network segmentation and identity boundaries — through configuration inspection and reliance on independent attestations such as SOC 2 or STAR. Accessing another tenant's data would itself violate isolation, sustainability reports are unrelated, and public CSPs do not expose rack-level placement to customers.

nodes.title: Compliance frameworks: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Compliance is the discipline of mapping your controls to an external framework (PCI, HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR, ISO 27001) and proving it to an auditor. Most exam questions test which framework owns which scope, not the minutiae of each clause.

flashcards.back: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard. Applies to anyone who stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data (PAN, expiry, CVV). 12 high-level requirements: firewalls, no defaults, encrypted storage, encrypted transmission, antivirus, secure dev, restrict access, MFA, log, test, policy. Required by Visa/Mastercard, not by law.

flashcards.front: HIPAA vs HITRUST — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: HIPAA is U.S. law for protected health information (PHI) — sets the legal requirements but is high-level on technical controls. HITRUST CSF is a certifiable framework that operationalizes HIPAA (plus ISO, NIST, PCI) into specific testable controls. Healthcare orgs are legally HIPAA-bound; many also pursue HITRUST cert to prove diligence.

American Institute of CPAs report on a SaaS company's controls across five trust criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy. Type I = controls designed at a point in time. Type II = controls operated effectively over 6-12 months. Enterprise customers ask for the Type II as proof you're not making it up.

flashcards.front: GDPR — what does it require beyond US-style privacy laws?
flashcards.back: European General Data Protection Regulation. Requires explicit consent (not pre-ticked), right to access / deletion / portability, 72-hour breach notification, data protection officer (for large processors), data minimization, and Privacy Impact Assessments for high-risk processing. Fines: up to 4% of global revenue. Applies to anyone processing EU residents' data, regardless of company location.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes the primary benefit of continuous auditing over traditional point-in-time auditing in cloud environments?
choices: It removes the need for the customer to maintain a control framework at all
It transfers legal accountability for compliance from the customer to the CSP
It provides near-real-time assurance that controls are operating effectively, better matching the rapid change rate of cloud services
It eliminates the requirement for any independent third-party attestation
questions.explanation: Continuous auditing uses automated tooling to gather and evaluate control evidence on an ongoing basis, giving near-real-time assurance rather than a periodic snapshot. This is a natural fit for cloud environments where configurations change constantly. It does not remove the need for a control framework or independent attestations, and it does not shift legal accountability — the customer remains accountable for its own compliance obligations.

questions.q: How many control domains does the Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4 contain?
questions.explanation: CCM v4 is organised into 17 control domains — including Audit & Assurance (A&A), Application & Interface Security (AIS), Business Continuity & Operational Resilience (BCR), Cryptography, Encryption & Key Management (CEK), Data Security & Privacy Lifecycle Management (DSP), Identity & Access Management (IAM), Interoperability & Portability (IPY), Logging & Monitoring (LOG), Security Incident Management (SEF), Supply-Chain Management (STA) and others. Earlier versions had fewer domains (CCM v3.0.1 had 16).

questions.q: An organisation processes EU-resident personal data in a public cloud region located outside the EU. From an auditor's perspective, which control area is the MOST important to evaluate?
choices: The provider's marketing claims about carbon-neutral operations
Whether the provider ships branded merchandise to the customer's employees
The colour scheme of the provider's management console
Lawful international data-transfer mechanisms (for example, EU Standard Contractual Clauses or an adequacy decision) and supporting technical/organisational measures
questions.explanation: Transferring EU-resident personal data outside the EU triggers GDPR Chapter V requirements. The auditor should test that a valid transfer mechanism is in place — an adequacy decision, Standard Contractual Clauses, or Binding Corporate Rules — supported by supplementary technical and organisational measures (encryption in transit and at rest, key management under the customer's control, minimisation) as recommended after the Schrems II ruling. The other options are irrelevant to the compliance risk.

questions.q: A cloud auditor's firm has been asked to perform a STAR-based attestation of the same CSP whose SIEM the firm also actively operates as a managed service. Which action BEST protects auditor independence?
choices: Proceed — providing managed services is normally considered a non-audit activity
Assign the attestation to a separately-governed team, or decline the engagement, so that the firm does not audit its own work
Disclose the relationship in the engagement letter and continue with the same team, because disclosure is sufficient
Rotate the individual auditor every two months while keeping the same delivery team on both engagements
questions.explanation: A core principle of auditor independence is that a firm must not audit its own work (a self-review threat). Operating the CSP's SIEM is a management-level service, so if the same firm attests to the CSP's controls it is effectively evaluating outputs it produced itself. Independence codes (for example the IESBA Code and ISACA's IT Audit Framework) require either using an independently-governed team behind an effective ethical wall or declining the engagement outright. Disclosure alone or personnel rotation does not remove the self-review threat.
